sentences.text: Milo ran back upstairs, oil lantern in one hand, single silver plate in the other.
He put both on the table by the door and looked at his father.
"Silver plates," he said.
"Great-grandmother Isla used silver plates behind an oil lantern.
There's only one plate in the cellar.
Where are the others?"
His father's eyes went wide.
Then narrowed, the way they did when he was remembering something from a long way back.
"The old parlor," he said.
"On the wall.
She hung them like decorations, so nobody would move them.
I never — I never thought to look."
The old parlor was a small room at the back of the cottage that nobody used anymore.
There were three framed pictures on the wall.
Milo had walked past them a thousand times without ever seeing them properly.
They were not pictures at all.
They were silver plates, hammered and polished, mounted in wooden frames.
Milo took them down.
Three of them.
Together with the one from the cellar, that was four.
He carried them up the tower with the lantern balanced on top like a stack of dinner things, and every time the wind hit the tower he thought the whole stack was going to fall.
In the lamp room, Milo set the plates on the floor and lit the oil lantern with a match.
The flame was small.
It looked hopeless.
He arranged the plates in a curve behind the lantern, the way Isla's note had said.
Silver caught the flame.
Silver doubled it, and doubled it again, and threw it back and forward and out through the glass wall of the lamp room.
Not as bright as the electric lamp had been.
Not close.
But visible.
Milo pressed his face against the glass and looked out across the black sea.
There.
A dark shape, low and long, coming out of the rain about a mile off.
The ferry from Oban.
It was tracking straight for the north face of Craighold Point — straight for the rocks.
Milo watched.
He held his breath.
The dark shape kept coming.
Then, slowly, it began to turn.
The captain of the ferry, later, said he had seen a strange light.
Not the usual lighthouse beam, but something softer.
Something that shimmered.
"It flickered like a candle," he told Milo's father, standing in the cottage the next morning with rain still on his coat.
"I have been sailing these waters for thirty years, and I have never seen a light like that.
But it was enough.
It was enough to know where I was."
Milo, sitting at the kitchen table with a mug of hot tea, did not say anything.
His mother had put Isla's note in a new frame.
It hung on the wall above the radio, where the pictures used to be.
That afternoon Milo's father, still bandaged, went into the cellar and got the small wooden box down from the shelf.
He took a fresh piece of paper.
He wrote on it for a long time in his careful, slow handwriting.
Then he folded it, put it in the box, and set the box back on the shelf, next to the oil lantern.
Milo watched him.
"What did you write?"
His father smiled.
It was tired and it was proud.
"I wrote the same kind of note Isla wrote," he said.
"For whoever comes next."
